noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the origin of carbon dioxide and oxygen as waste products of metabolism and their loss from the stomata of a leaf

primer.text: Plants run two gas-hungry processes on opposite schedules: photosynthesis in the daylight hours and respiration around the clock. The result is that each gas takes its turn as surplus, and the leaf simply lets the excess drift away through its stomata — no pumping, no effort, just diffusion.

lessons.title: Plant Wastes and the Stomata
sourceHeadings: The Need for Excretion in Plants
lessons.opening: Plant metabolism produces two wastes worth naming: oxygen, surplus in the light, and carbon dioxide, surplus in the dark. In bright daylight a photosynthesising leaf burns through carbon dioxide faster than respiration replaces it, and the oxygen it makes piles up until it leaks away through the stomata. When darkness falls the roles reverse and carbon dioxide now accumulates and drifts out. Because the gases simply move down their gradients, the process costs the plant no energy.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis and respiration in a plant can each turn the other's raw material into waste.
In bright light photosynthesis outruns respiration, so oxygen is the surplus gas.
In darkness only respiration runs, so carbon dioxide is the surplus gas.
The surplus gas diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata.
Diffusion costs no energy, so plant gas excretion is a passive process.

low.restatement: Whatever gas the plant is not using at the moment diffuses out through the stomata.
low.analogy: It is like a revolving door that only swings when more people push from one side.
low.examPointer: State the direction of the net gas flow for day and for night — both are commonly asked.

medium.restatement: Light decides which gas is waste: oxygen by day, carbon dioxide by night.
medium.analogy: Two clocks run at once — the solar-powered one and the always-on one — and the faster one sets the waste.
medium.examPointer: Quote the phrase net effect when comparing the two rates, as mark schemes reward it.

check.stem: Which gas do plants excrete in daylight?

options.text: Oxygen, because photosynthesis produces more than respiration uses
options.explanation: Surplus oxygen from faster photosynthesis is the daylight waste.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, because photosynthesis makes it
options.explanation: Photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide; it releases oxygen.
Nitrogen plays no part in plant metabolism here.
Transpiration happens, but the excretion asked about is the gas pair.

check.stem: What do plants do with carbon dioxide at night?

options.text: They produce it by respiration and it diffuses out
options.explanation: Respiration runs without light, so carbon dioxide becomes the surplus gas.

options.text: They absorb extra carbon dioxide for storage
options.explanation: Nothing stores it; in darkness the plant makes more than it can use.

options.text: They stop producing any waste at all
options.explanation: Respiration never stops, so waste keeps coming.
Conversion needs photosynthesis, which has stopped.

check.stem: Why is gas excretion in plants a passive process?

options.text: The gases simply diffuse down their concentration gradients
options.explanation: No pump or transport protein is needed; the gradient does the work.

options.text: Because the stomata are always wide open
options.explanation: Stomata open and close; openness is not the passivity.
Thinness speeds diffusion but does not make it passive.
Photosynthesis creates the gradient; the diffusion itself is unpowered.

check.stem: During a bright day, what is the net effect on the two gases?

options.text: More oxygen produced than used, and less carbon dioxide released than used
options.explanation: Photosynthesis dominates, so oxygen accumulates and carbon dioxide is drawn down.

options.text: More carbon dioxide produced than used
options.explanation: That is the night-time balance.
Exact balance happens at a particular low light intensity, not in bright light.
Both keep moving; only the net balance shifts.

check.stem: Through which structures do the waste gases leave the leaf?

options.explanation: The stomata are the pores the gases drift through.
Roots take up water and ions; they are not this exit.
The cuticle is a barrier, not a pore.
Xylem carries water upwards inside the plant.

check.stem: Name the two waste gases of plant metabolism.
State when each gas becomes surplus in a plant.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen is surplus in the light when photosynthesis outruns respiration; carbon dioxide is surplus in the dark when only respiration runs.

check.stem: Explain why the same gas can be a raw material by day and a waste by night.
check.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen while light lasts, but in darkness only respiration runs, consuming oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide; the direction of the faster process decides which gas is in surplus, so each gas swaps roles as the light changes.

check.stem: A greenhouse keeper keeps lights on all night. Predict the gas exchange and explain why.
check.modelAnswer: With light supplied, photosynthesis continues through the night, so the plant keeps consuming carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen; the usual night-time pattern of net carbon dioxide release is replaced by a daytime-style exchange in which oxygen is the surplus gas.

glossary.definition: A pore in the leaf epidermis, formed between two guard cells, through which gases diffuse in and out.
The overall direction of gas movement once the faster of photosynthesis and respiration has set the balance.
A movement driven only by a concentration gradient, costing the cell no energy.
